anchor: To test whether a layer verified in Lean 4
comment: Reply (proved or proven): both are accepted past participles. Formal-methods writing says proved (proved correct), and proven is the usual adjective (a proven method). Where the word stood as an adjective, as in a proved layer, I changed it to verified, which the title already uses. Proved to meet, what is proved, and the Table 1 status Proved stay.

anchor: clinician validation and a held-out round remain.
comment: Reply (what these entail): Clinician validation means a pharmacist or clinician, your mentor or the clinical co-author, checks the four label-dose thresholds, the route and unit code tables, the 16 same-ingredient pairs, and the questionable faithful lines listed in Supplementary Section S10, and relabels a blind sample of released texts so we can report human agreement with the model labels. Your own labeling covers the blind sample, but a reviewer will still want a clinician's name on the dosing checks. A held-out round means a new adversarial round (h3) written by fresh instances against version 2.1 frozen at the release tag, with a file manifest, labeled and reported as found, with no code change until the labels are in. Both fit before submission; h3 is about a day of work. I have proposed h3 and the labeling tool as separate tasks that start on your go.

anchor: Formal verification has been used in medicine before, to prove properties of the software in infusion pumps
comment: Reply (infusion pumps): reworded to say what was verified and why it is the nearest precedent. Reference 7 is a formally developed infusion pump controller; reference 5 is Thimbleby's work on the number-entry keypads of medical devices, where a misread decimal point changes a dose tenfold.

anchor: has not, to our knowledge, been examined
comment: Reply (we as a sole author): we and our are conventional and accepted for a single author in JAMIA, and they become literally true if the clinical co-author joins. I left them and changed the three phrases that said the authors' judgment to the singular, which the Methods already used. If you publish alone and prefer no plural, say so and I will recast those sentences.

anchor: with machine-checked proofs that each drug name, dose, route, frequency, and daily total in its released text equals the matching field of the active order it names
comment: Reply (written specification; proved or proven; what stops the model): the sentence now says what the specification is, and the next two sentences say why the model cannot state an amount or a drug name: the layer rejects any output containing a digit, a number, unit, route, or frequency word, or any word outside the 67-word vocabulary and the four sentence shapes, so an amount reaches the patient only through a slot the layer fills from the order. Proved here is the participle (proved to have these properties), which is standard. Figure 1, new, with its legend after the references, shows the same flow.

anchor: render, the function that turns the model's text and the orders into released text or a block reason
comment: Reply (what render means): render is the layer's main function. It takes the model's text and the patient's orders and returns either the text to release or the reason for blocking. It is now defined here and in the Methods paragraph on the specification.

anchor: no proof is a placeholder (sorry) or rests on running compiled code (native_decide)
comment: Reply (sorry and native_decide): jargon, now spelled out. In Lean, sorry is a placeholder that lets a file compile with a proof missing, and native_decide proves a statement by running compiled code instead of checking it in the kernel. Neither appears in the development, and the continuous integration check enforces that on every push.

anchor: 270 regression tests, each a fixed request with an expected reply; on 20,000 mutated requests of 53 kinds the reader agrees with a separate Python program that follows the same written rules
comment: Reply (explain again): the reader is the code that turns the patient's FHIR orders into the values the proofs reason about. It is not proved, so it is tested two ways: 270 regression tests, each a fixed request with a known expected reply, and a fuzz test that mutates requests 20,000 times and checks that the Lean reader and a separate Python program written from the same rules give the same answer. That shows the reader follows its rules, not that the rules are right. The Methods paragraph before Table 1 now says this in those words.

anchor: the development rounds are in Supplementary Section S5
comment: Reply (publish the working system): done. Version 1 and round h1 no longer appear in the main text; this pointer is all that remains, and Supplementary Section S5 and Table S5a hold the development rounds, the held-out round h1, and the lesson that correct proofs did not rescue a loose specification.

anchor: every label was assigned by an instance of Claude, and no clinician labeled any output
comment: Reply (you labeling): yes. I have proposed a labeling task for you to start. It will give you a schema (faithful; misstates an order, with the error type; unsupported claim; plus the same-ingredient flag), a blind queue that shows each released text beside its active orders with the model labels hidden, and an export that computes your agreement with the model labels for this paragraph and for the clinical validation placeholder in Limitations. The sample: the 9 misstatements, 4 unsupported claims, 30 faithful texts, and 16 same-ingredient pairs from round h2, the 60 sampled open-model releases, and the 74 Claude free-daily flags, about 170 items.

anchor: Two hosted models from Anthropic, Claude Haiku 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5, ran through the Messages API
comment: Reply (test up to Fable): Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1 can run through the same harness on the 120 cases and four conditions. Haiku and Sonnet together cost about $1.73, so the two larger models should cost roughly $10 to $40 together. Table 4 would then carry seven model columns and may need to turn sideways. I have proposed this as a task; it starts on your go. The settings to confirm first: low effort, a 2,000-token limit including thinking, no temperature sent, no sampled condition, and no labeler reading their outputs.
